<reason>In an exceptionally high-level debate, Side B won by systematically dismantling Side A's institutional mechanics and winning the comparison of failure modes. Side B turned Side A's government-funding analogy into proof that calendar deadlines invite hostage-taking, neutralized Side A's procedural objections to affirmative revocation via minority-triggered privileged resolutions, and forced Side A to concede that swing-vote extortion can cause powers to lapse under a sunset. When Side A tried to minimize that lapse as a harmless "day of argument" before re-passage, Side B convincingly showed why a 24-hour legal vacuum during a banking panic, quarantine, or security crisis causes irreversible chaos.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's sequence in [B3.1], [B4.1], and [B4.4]: after Side A argued fast-track rules could prevent renewal blockades [A3.1], Side B distinguished procedural bottlenecks from substantive swing-vote extortion at midnight, forced Side A to concede that hostage-taking lapses can happen [A4.1], and then demolished Side A's claim that emergency powers evaporating for "a day" is harmless.</best_rebuttal>
